KEY MESSAGE 1... An active and unsettled pattern begins today,  
with a Marginal Risk for severe weather and Excessive Rainfall. 

As a strong upper-level ridge expands into the Plains early 
this week, northwesterly flow aloft will occur across much of 
the East. This ridge gets pushed back some as a strong upper- 
level trough in eastern Canada sends spokes of energy 
southeastward across the Great Lakes and Northeast. Some 
guidance maintains a vigorous shortwave riding over the ridge 
and sliding southeastward across the Great Lakes today and then
across the Northeast during Tuesday. This results in some model
solutions continuing to close off the trough across the 
Northeast Tuesday into Wednesday. Some other guidance is slower 
and weaker and thus does not close it off or briefly closes it 
off a day or two later. The upper-level system will drive 
surface low pressure and a cold front our way Tuesday into 
Wednesday. It will become much more humid during the first half 
of next week, with dew points looking to surge on Tuesday.

These factors will lead to the development of showers and
thunderstorms across the area today. The latest radar images as
of 1140AM show that the first echos have already developed. 
The setup looks to be a pulsy, single to multi cell cluster 
environment with low shear and modest instability, similar to 
what we have seen early this morning with some severe 
thunderstorms over the Eastern Shore of MD. Deep layer shear 
will be weak, only around 10-20 kts. Instability looks to be in 
the 1000-2000 J/kg range. DCAPE is also modest around 500-1000 
J/kg. This setup will favor scattered, hit or miss type showers 
and thunderstorms developing during the afternoon hours, with a 
marginal risk of severe thunderstorms. Any stronger storms could
produce isolated strong to marginally severe wind gusts and 
brief heavy downpours. CAMs have been focusing development 
mainly along the sea and bay breezes, but lingering outflow 
boundaries from convection this morning could also be the nexus 
for convective initiation. Our entire area is outlooked in a 
MARGINAL Risk (level 1 out of 5) for severe thunderstorms today.
An excessive rainfall outlook was reintroduced across Delaware
and a sliver of the eastern shore of MD as of 11AM. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Most impactful weather likely comes on Tuesday 
with the highest chance for severe weather and flash flooding. 
Unsettled weather continues through mid-week though .

Tuesday looks to feature the most widespread showers and
thunderstorms. Height falls and jet dynamics aloft will favor
convective development nearly all day as surface low pressure 
develops just to our west. This will keep a steady stream of 
warm, moist air pumping into the area and keeping the 
environment conditionally unstable despite cloud cover. PWats 
will rise to near 2" by the end of the day. Some models suggest
we could have a stalled or slow moving frontal boundary across
the central or northern portion of the forecast area, which
could act as a focusing mechanism for heavy rainfall. Heavy 
rain leading to flash flooding could end up being a bigger 
concern and greater impact than the severe thunderstorm threat.

Long story short, a very active day is expected convection 
wise on Tuesday. A due southerly surface flow and the dynamics 
aloft will favor areas along and northwest of the I-95 corridor
and/or the frontal boundary to be the focus of the heaviest 
rain, and areas along and southeast of the I-95 corridor and/or
the frontal boundary where convection is less messy and the 
environment a bit less contaminated being the greater severe 
thunderstorm threat depending on exactly how the convection 
evolves. That still remains a little unclear at the moment, and 
may depend on how storms evolve upstream Monday and Monday 
night.

WPC has outlooked most of our area outside of central/southern
Delmarva in a SLIGHT Risk (level 2 out of 4) for excessive 
rainfall for Tuesday. SPC has outlooked the southern half of our
area from the Philly metro and south in a SLIGHT Risk (level 2 
out of 5) for severe thunderstorms on Tuesday.

On Wednesday, low pressure looks to be offshore to our east. 
Scattered showers and storms will likely develop again by 
afternoon, at least across our NJ and PA zones, but the severe 
thunderstorm threat will be lower given lower instability. Will
have to monitor the flash flood threat though as WPC has added
the northern part of our area in a SLIGHT (Level 2/4) Risk for
excessive rainfall with a MARGINAL (1/4) Risk elsewhere. 

As we head through Thursday and Friday, the risk of scattered
showers and storms will slowly decline as the Tuesday-Wednesday 
system slowly pushes east. Details on the late week period are 
still very uncertain, however. We may briefly dry out completely 
Saturday before the next system approaches Sunday.
